content: 1. Ischemic heart disease, which is caused by blocked or narrowed arteries, is a current condition that requires careful management. 2. A history of stroke is a significant medical concern that must be considered in clinical decision-making. 3. The presence of multiple risk factors for arterial cardiovascular disease, such as diabetes and hypertension, increases the likelihood of complications. 4. Unexplained vaginal bleeding should be thoroughly evaluated to rule out any serious underlying conditions before proceeding with treatment. 5. A history of breast cancer that occurred more than five years ago and has not recurred is an important consideration in assessing patient eligibility for certain therapies. 6. Long-standing diabetes (over 20 years) or diabetes-related complications affecting the arteries, vision, kidneys, or nervous system require specialized care. 7. Severe cirrhosis or the presence of a liver tumor is a contraindication for certain medical interventions. 8. Systemic lupus erythematosus with positive or unknown antiphospholipid antibodies, especially in the absence of immunosuppressive treatment, or severe thrombocytopenia, necessitates careful evaluation before initiating specific treatments. Guidance for Continuing Users of Injectable Contraceptives (DMPA): 1. During follow-up visits, inquire about the client’s experience with the method and whether she is satisfied. Address any questions or concerns she may have. 2. Specifically ask if she has noticed any changes in bleeding patterns and provide relevant information or assistance as needed. 3. Administer the DMPA injection or provide supplies for self-injection. Note that the injection can be given up to four weeks late if necessary. 4. Plan the next injection date, typically in three months or 13 weeks for DMPA. Encourage timely visits but emphasize that she should return even if delayed. 5. For long-term users, ask about any new health problems and address them appropriately. 6. Discuss major life changes, such as plans for having children or changes in STI/HIV risk, and provide follow-up care as needed. DMPA-SC Injectable Contraceptive: 1. DMPA-SC, also known as Depo-SubQ Provera or Sayana Press, is a progestin-only injectable contraceptive. It contains a hormone similar to natural progesterone and is administered subcutaneously (just under the skin). 2. It works primarily by preventing ovulation (the release of eggs from the ovaries). 3. DMPA-SC can be self-injected and is available in two systems: the Uniject device (Sayana Press) and prefilled syringes (Depo-Provera). Both use short needles for subcutaneous administration. 4. Effectiveness depends on regular injections. When used correctly, fewer than 1 in 100 women will become pregnant in the first year. 5. Fertility typically returns about four months after stopping DMPA, which is longer than most other contraceptive methods. 6. DMPA does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Side Effects of DMPA-SC: 1. Common side effects include irregular bleeding, prolonged bleeding, or no monthly bleeding over time. 2. Other reported effects include weight gain, headaches, dizziness, abdominal bloating, mood changes, and reduced libido. 3. There may also be a loss of bone density with prolonged use. 4. These side effects are not indicative of illness, and many women do not experience them. Clients should be encouraged to return for help if side effects are bothersome. NET-EN Injectable Contraceptive: 1. NET-EN, also known as Norethisterone Enanthate, is a progestin-only injectable contraceptive administered intramuscularly. 2. It works by preventing ovulation and is effective when injections are given on schedule. 3. Fertility typically returns about one month after stopping NET-EN, which is shorter than with DMPA. 4. NET-EN affects bleeding patterns less than DMPA, with fewer days of bleeding in the first six months and a lower likelihood of no monthly bleeding after one year. 5. Common side effects include irregular bleeding, weight gain, headaches, dizziness, abdominal bloating, mood changes, and reduced libido. 6. NET-EN offers protection against pregnancy and may reduce the risk of iron-deficiency anemia. Progestogen-Only Pills (POPs): 1. POPs, also known as “minipills,” contain low doses of progestin and do not include estrogen. They are suitable for breastfeeding women and those who cannot use estrogen-containing methods. 2. POPs work by thickening cervical mucus to block sperm and disrupting the menstrual cycle, including preventing ovulation. 3. Effectiveness depends on consistent daily use. Breastfeeding women have a lower risk of pregnancy (less than 1 in 100 in the first year), while non-breastfeeding women have a slightly higher risk (about 7 in 100). 4. Fertility returns quickly after stopping POPs. Clinical Judgment in Special Cases: 1. Women with certain conditions, such as severe hypertension, recent childbirth (less than six weeks postpartum), or a history of heart disease, should generally avoid progestin-only injectables unless no other suitable options are available. 2. Providers must carefully assess the severity of the condition and ensure access to follow-up care before prescribing these methods.
